(This evening through Wednesday)...
Issued at 221 PM EST Wed Nov 11 2026

A positively tilted shortwave will aid in the development of a 
surface low, of which will pass through central Indiana later today 
through tonight. Satellite imagery shows a well defined warm frontal 
boundary with modest elevated instability just to the north. There 
is a faintly defined cold front developing along/near the 
Mississippi, but it is in the very early stages of FGEN with mainly 
low level convergence as the primary driver. As the day progresses, 
diurnal/differential heating along with low level pressure depletion 
will aid in some additional FGEN, but without strong temperature 
advection, the overall low pressure system will likely remain 
relatively immature until after is pushes east of central Indiana. 

Without strong temperature advection, the primary driver for today's 
convective threat will likely default to modest vorticity advection 
and low level pressure depletion just ahead of the shortwave. 
Current observations showcase an amplified and concentrated area of 
CVA across IA/IL, but RAP analysis is indicating that this will 
become for diffuse as the day progresses, with a more broadly 
defined area of CVA this afternoon and evening. Pressure depletion 
is likely to follow closely to the already defined warm front of 
which is currently over northern portions of central Indiana. This 
is where we expected the greatest concentration of convection to 
occur, with mores scattered to isolated cells developing south of 
this area over the rest of central Indiana. 

Regarding the severe threat today, the primary concern is for 
consistent small hail and isolated damaging wind gusts. While 
tornadoes cannot be completely ruled out, the lack of low level 
directional shear along with a fairly dry and well mixed PBL will 
inhibit tornadogenisis considerably. If a tornado were to occur, it 
will likely be near or along the frontal boundary where locally 
enhanced backing is observer, or where cell mergers occur within a 
more organized convective cluster. 

The main focus for damaging winds is expected to be along the I-74 
corridor where greater mid level dynamics will likely aid in 
convective organization, tapping into a very dry mid level layer. 
Outside of this area, very isolated damaging winds cannot be ruled 
out, but should mostly be contained to 35-45MPH winds within sparse 
convective cells. Small hail is likely to be fairly prolific within 
strong cells today due to the HGZ well within the area of steep 
lapse rates (7.2-7.7C/km). Weak shear within this layer along with a 
shallow corridor of CAPE is likely to keep most hail stones below 
1". That said, there is a low end threat for these smaller hail 
stones to congeal together to create large hail clusters. We will 
watch for this within strong convective updrafts where numerous 
cells are merging.

After the low passes to the east overnight, strong NW flow is 
expected to develop as the PBL maintains instability beneath modest 
CAA. Gusts are expected to peak around 30-35MPH, with consistent 
gusts around 25MPH. This NW flow will push much cooler air into the 
region with the coldest air of the Fall arriving for Thursday and 
Friday. This cold air will be further reinforced by an amplifying 
upper trough with a close low developing over the eastern Great 
Lakes by Friday night. Multiple waves will pivot around the flank of 
the upper level trough maintaining plenty of low level clouds and 
periodic precipitation through the period.

The strongest of the short waves will track across the region on 
Thursday. As it does so the wave will interact with strong cold 
advection and steepening mid level lapse rates to generate scattered 
to numerous light rain showers peaking in coverage during the 
afternoon and focused particularly across the northeast half of the 
forecast area. The addition of brisk northwest winds and broad 
stratus will make for a raw chilly day across the area with highs 
remaining in the 40s. 

A strong upper level trough will continue to remain in place during 
the day Friday. Despite limited moisture with dew points in the 
upper 20's to low 30's, 15-25 kts of cold NNW flow off of Lake 
Michigan supports the development of a north-to-south oriented band 
of precipitation extending down towards the I-70 corridor. Even with 
temperatures in the mid 30's to low 40's at the surface, freezing 
temperatures just above the surface support the potential of a few 
embedded snow showers and/or graupel. 

The upper level trough is expected to shift east starting Saturday 
bringing with it the transition to a ridging pattern that is 
expected to persist through the end of next week. Other than some 
scattered lingering cloud cover Saturday and Sunday, next week will 
bring the return of more quiet seasonable weather and mainly sunny 
skies. High temperatures next week will range in the 40's through 
upper 50's with lows in the low to mid 30's
